prompt: You run `az container create` with one image and nothing else unusual. What does Azure create?
hint: Think about which resource is named, billed and deleted.

choices.text: A virtual machine of yours, sized to the image, that runs it
choices.why: There is no machine of yours: the host is Microsoft's and you never see it.

choices.text: A container group holding one container
choices.why: The group is the top-level resource, and a group of one is the common case.

choices.text: A single container, with no group, since a group needs two
choices.why: A group of one container is still a group; every setting belongs to it or to its container.

choices.text: A pod in an AKS cluster that Azure manages for you
choices.why: Container Instances has no cluster around the group; AKS is lesson 11.

prompt: The shop and a monitoring sidecar run in one container group. Which of these do the two containers share? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four things are shared; the list has three of them.

choices.text: The host they are placed on
choices.why: The containers of a group are scheduled on one machine.

choices.text: A public IP address each, so either can be called directly
choices.why: The group has one address; the containers behind it are told apart by port.

choices.text: `localhost`, on any port, opened or not
choices.why: That is how the sidecar reaches `localhost:8080/healthz` without an address of its own.

choices.text: A separate bill per container, by its own running time
choices.why: The group is billed as one, for what its containers request, while any of them runs.

choices.text: A lifecycle: they start, stop and restart together
choices.why: Restarting or updating the group restarts every container in it.

prompt: A Linux container group has three containers, requesting 1.5 GB, 0.5 GB and 1 GB of memory, and none sets a limit. How many gigabytes of memory is the group allocated?
hint: The group's allocation is built from its containers' requests.

prompt: The report job must be reachable from the office over a VPN, and the team also wants it on a public DNS name. Can one container group do both?
hint: Read the rules that come with a group in a virtual network.

choices.text: Yes, once the subnet has been delegated to Container Instances
choices.why: Delegation is what lets a group into the subnet at all; it adds no public face.

choices.text: Yes, if the DNS label is added after the group is in the subnet
choices.why: The CLI refuses `--dns-name-label` with `--vnet`, and Azure's own rule is the same: no label in a virtual network.

choices.text: No: a group in a virtual network gets no public address and no DNS label
choices.why: It is one or the other. A public face for a private group comes from something in front of it.

choices.text: Yes, as long as the NAT gateway has a public IP address
choices.why: The NAT gateway carries the group's outgoing connections; nothing comes in through it.

prompt: A partner's system calls the shop's group at its public IP address, which they copied into their configuration. What will go wrong, and what should they use?
hint: What does Microsoft say about the address when a group restarts?

choices.text: Nothing: the address belongs to the group until the group is deleted
choices.why: It is released on deletion, and it can also change when the group restarts.

choices.text: It is not fixed across restarts; they should use the DNS label
choices.why: The label, `shop-sp.brazilsouth.azurecontainer.io`, is the stable half.

choices.text: Every group in the region shares the address; they need to add the port
choices.why: A group's public address is its own; the port was needed anyway.

choices.text: The address is rotated daily, so they should look it up again every morning
choices.why: There is no schedule. It may change on a restart, which is why nothing should hold it.

prompt: Why does `app.py` listen on `0.0.0.0` rather than `127.0.0.1`?
hint: Where does a request published with `-p 8080:8080` arrive from, as the container sees it?

choices.text: `0.0.0.0` puts the shop on the internet; `127.0.0.1` keeps it on the laptop
choices.why: Binding to every interface inside the container exposes nothing by itself; publishing a port does that.

choices.text: `ThreadingHTTPServer` refuses `127.0.0.1` when it runs as `nobody`
choices.why: Any user may listen on the loopback address; the problem is who can reach it.

choices.text: A server on `127.0.0.1` inside a container cannot be reached from outside it
choices.why: Requests arrive on the container's network interface, and the loopback address is not on it.

choices.text: Docker rewrites `127.0.0.1` to the host's address, so both would work
choices.why: Docker rewrites nothing in the program; the second call in the sidecar transcript shows what a separate `localhost` means.

prompt: The second `docker run`, started without `--network container:shop`, asked `http://localhost:8080/healthz` and got `Connection refused`. Why?
hint: Whose `localhost` was it?

choices.text: Its `localhost` was its own, and nothing was listening on 8080 there
choices.why: Without the flag it has a network of its own; with it, it shares the shop's, as a group does.

choices.text: The shop accepts connections only from containers of another image
choices.why: Both containers used `shop:1.0`, and the first call was answered.

choices.text: The shop was still answering the first call and turned the second away
choices.why: `ThreadingHTTPServer` answers each request on its own thread; nothing was queued.

choices.text: `USER nobody` may not open network connections inside a container
choices.why: The first call ran as `nobody` too, and it was answered.

prompt: Docker's flag `--network ___:shop` starts a new one inside the network of the running `shop`, the arrangement a group gives its members.
hint: The word Docker uses for what it runs.

prompt: Put the steps of running the shop on your laptop in order.
hint: Files, then an image, then a container, then traffic, then what it wrote.
items: Build the image with `docker build --tag shop:1.0 shop`
Start it with `docker run -d --name shop -p 8080:8080 shop:1.0`
Read the request's line with `docker logs shop`
trap: The log line for a request exists only after the request; `docker logs` before any `curl` shows only the line printed on starting.

prompt: A developer builds `shop:1.0` on a Mac with Apple silicon, pushes it, and the container group in Azure fails to start. What is the most likely cause?
hint: Which processors does Container Instances run images for?

choices.text: `python:3.12-slim` is not one of the base images Azure allows
choices.why: Any image in a registry Azure can reach may be used; nothing restricts the base.

choices.text: The image is `arm64` only, and Container Instances runs x64 images
choices.why: Build it with `--platform linux/amd64`; Microsoft says an `arm64`-only image may fail to start.

choices.text: Container Instances refuses an image whose `Dockerfile` says `USER nobody`
choices.why: Running as a user other than root is allowed; only an Azure Files mount needs root.

choices.text: Port 8080 is one of the ports Container Instances reserves for itself
choices.why: The reserved list includes 22 and 3389 and does not include 8080.

prompt: A colleague creates the shop's group with `--image`, `--ip-address Public` and `--dns-name-label shop-sp`, and no other flags. It runs, and nobody can reach it. Why?
hint: Read the default of one flag in the help text.

choices.text: Without `--cpu` and `--memory` the group starts with no resources at all
choices.why: The group ran; a group too small to run would not be shown running.

choices.text: A DNS label takes a day to be published, so the name is not answering yet
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation describes a delay like that, and the IP address would not answer either.

choices.text: A public group needs a load balancer before any traffic reaches it
choices.why: A public group is reached directly at its address; a load balancer is for several groups.

choices.text: With no `--ports`, the CLI opens port 80, and the shop listens on 8080
choices.why: The help says `Default: [80]`. The group answers nobody on 80 and has 8080 closed.

prompt: Match each workload to the restart policy that fits it.
hint: Ask what should happen after a clean exit, and after a failed one.

pairs.left: The order API, which should never stop
The nightly report, retried if it crashes, finished once it succeeds
A job that must not start again after it succeeded

prompt: A Bicep file with `restartPolicy: 'OnFaliure'` compiled with no warning, and the same word given to `az container create` was refused. What do the two answers tell you?
hint: Which of the two carries its own list of allowed values?

choices.text: The compiler corrected the spelling in the template, so the file is safe
choices.why: `jq` read `OnFaliure` back out of `typo.json`; nothing was corrected.

choices.text: The CLI is out of date, and API version `2025-09-01` added the word
choices.why: No such policy exists; the three are `Always`, `OnFailure` and `Never`.

choices.text: Azure treats an unknown policy as `Always`, so the group will still run
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation says what Azure does with it; only a deployment would show.

choices.text: The compiler accepts any text there, so that value is yours to check
choices.why: Its types allow the three words and any other text; the CLI checks its own list.

prompt: A group has two containers, each requesting 1 CPU. One of them runs heavier work and is given a CPU limit. What is the highest limit, in CPUs, it may be given?
hint: A limit can reach as far as what the whole group was allocated.

prompt: The report's group was created with `Always` by mistake, and every night it starts the report again as soon as it finishes. How is it changed to `OnFailure`?
hint: Some properties of a group cannot be updated in place.

choices.text: Delete the group and create it again with `OnFailure`
choices.why: The restart policy is one of the properties that need the group deleted first, with CPU, memory, the OS type, the network profile and the zone.

choices.text: Run the create again with `--restart-policy OnFailure`, and the containers restart in place
choices.why: That is how an updatable property changes; the restart policy is not one of them.

choices.text: Run `az container restart` with the new policy, which applies from the next start
choices.why: A restart re-runs the group with the configuration it has; it takes no new policy.

choices.text: Stop the group, change the policy, and start it again, keeping its address
choices.why: A stopped group cannot be edited into another policy, and its address was never guaranteed anyway.

prompt: Which of the shop's workloads fits a container group worst?
hint: Which one has customers waiting on it all day, through every deployment?

choices.text: The nightly sales report
choices.why: A job that runs, writes a file and exits is the case Container Instances is best at.

choices.text: The order API
choices.why: It needs copies under load and updates without a break, and a group has neither.

choices.text: The monthly finance export
choices.why: Another job: started, finished, billed for its minutes.

choices.text: A developer's test run for a pull request
choices.why: A container that runs the tests and stops is the build-agent case Microsoft names.

prompt: Which of these does a single container group NOT give you on its own? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three things an orchestrator does are missing.

choices.text: A second copy started when the first is busy
choices.why: A group keeps no count; more groups are yours to create.

choices.text: A job that stops being billed once it has finished
choices.why: With `OnFailure` or `Never`, a finished group stops, and so does its meter.

choices.text: A new version deployed with no break in service
choices.why: An update restarts every container in place, and nobody answers meanwhile.

choices.text: One address in front of several copies of the shop
choices.why: A group has no load balancer of its own; Microsoft documents adding a Standard Load Balancer in a virtual network.

choices.text: A sidecar that reaches the shop on `localhost`
choices.why: That is exactly what a group gives its containers.

prompt: The report's image is built like the shop's, with `USER nobody`, and it mounts an Azure Files share for its output. What does Microsoft's documentation say about that combination?
hint: The documentation puts one condition on the user inside the container.

choices.text: An Azure Files mount requires the container to run as root
choices.why: So the report's image cannot run as `nobody`, and that is a trade to make knowingly.

choices.text: It works only if the group is in a virtual network
choices.why: A share can be mounted by a public group too; a virtual network adds a service endpoint requirement, not this.

choices.text: The share can be mounted only read-only by a user other than root
choices.why: Read-only is a setting of the mount, not a consequence of the user.

choices.text: Azure Files can be mounted only into Windows containers
choices.why: The reverse: volume mounts, Azure Files included, are Linux only.

prompt: An AKS cluster has a virtual node backed by Container Instances. A pod is scheduled onto it. What runs where?
hint: Which of the two is the orchestrator here?

choices.text: Container Instances takes over scheduling for the whole cluster
choices.why: Kubernetes still schedules; the virtual node is one more place it can put a pod.

choices.text: Azure adds a virtual machine to the cluster faster than the autoscaler would
choices.why: No virtual machine is added; that is the wait the virtual node avoids.

choices.text: The pod runs as a container group in Container Instances, placed there by Kubernetes
choices.why: The node registers with unlimited capacity, and its pods run as groups billed by the second.

choices.text: The pod runs on the AKS nodes, and Container Instances only holds its image
choices.why: Images live in a registry; the pod itself runs in Container Instances.

prompt: NGroups keeps a declared number of container groups, each made from one template called a container group ___.
hint: The word for a template of settings that many groups are made from.

prompt: A Bicep file declares a Spot container group in `brazilsouth`, and it compiles without a warning. What does Microsoft's documentation say about deploying it?
hint: The compiler knows types. What does it not know?

choices.text: Spot is a preview offered in East US 2, West Europe and West US only
choices.why: The compiler checks types, not where a feature is offered.

choices.text: It deploys, with the eviction policy set to delete unless another is chosen
choices.why: Spot groups have no eviction policy to choose; an evicted group is restarted by Azure.

choices.text: It deploys, and receives a public address as soon as capacity is found
choices.why: A Spot group gets no public address at all in this preview.

choices.text: It deploys in São Paulo, and Spot is just a lower priority there
choices.why: The documentation lists three regions, and São Paulo is not one of them.

prompt: The report's group failed last Tuesday and has been stopped since. Somebody wants its full log from that night. What will they find?
hint: Look at what is kept for a running group and for a stopped one.

choices.text: The whole log, kept for 30 days after the group has stopped
choices.why: No such retention is documented; a stopped group keeps far less.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because a stopped group's log is deleted with it
choices.why: Something is kept, but only 16 KB or 1,000 lines of it.

choices.text: At most 16 KB or 1,000 lines, unless it went to Log Analytics
choices.why: A running group keeps 4 MB and a stopped one less; a workspace keeps the rest.

choices.text: The log of each restart, in a separate file per attempt
choices.why: No per-attempt files are described; the group's log is small and bounded.

prompt: The nightly report runs in a group with `OnFailure`, crashes once and then succeeds. Put what happens in order.
hint: The meter starts before the program does.
items: The first image starts downloading, and the meter starts
The report runs and exits with code 1
The report writes its file and exits with code 0
The group shows as Terminated, and the meter stops
trap: Exit code 0 is the end under `OnFailure`; nothing restarts the container after that.

prompt: The shop runs in one container group. You deploy `shop:1.1` by running the create again with the new image. What do customers see?
hint: How does an update treat the containers of a group?

choices.text: Nothing: Azure starts 1.1 beside 1.0 and moves the traffic once it is healthy
choices.why: That is a rolling update, and a single group has none.

choices.text: Nothing, because an update applies only to the next restart
choices.why: An update restarts the containers at once.

choices.text: A refusal, because the image is a property that cannot be updated
choices.why: The image can be updated in place; CPU, memory and the restart policy cannot.

choices.text: A break while every container restarts in place, with nothing else answering
choices.why: One group, no second copy, and an update restarts all its containers.
